content:
Hi everyone! I am new to this community, but I've been "learning by doing" with a couple projects, especially around chip firing games on graphs.

I'm hoping to interest others in a project Dhyey Mavani and I have recently worked on, in which we formalized the Baker and Norine's Riemann Roch theorem for finite graphs. Along the way, we formalized some basic results in chipfiring game / sandpiles, including Dhar's burning algorithm and the existence of q-reduced divisors (chip configurations).

We're hoping that some parts of this project may be suitable for Mathlib, but need some help from more experienced people. Our repo is here:

https://github.com/DhyeyMavani2003/chip-firing-with-lean

We would love suggestions on this work, or perhaps collaborators. We do anticipate several challenges in getting it "Mathlib ready." Notably: we began the work in 2024, before Mathlib had a multigraph definition. It now has that definition, so we'll need to refactor our code to use it. Also, the repo is quite big right now, and I imagine it will need to go in in smaller, more reviewable chunks.

Some concrete questions:

  • Is this work, or part of it, a suitable candidate for a PR down the road?
  • What are some natural "first steps" in this direction?
  • Does anyone want to work on this with us?
Hi and welcome --- it's great to have new members here. Looking at your repository, I wonder to what extent you used AI to generate it. Can you tell us more?

I am asking because this influence the advice I'd give. Importantly, mathlib has very high standards and at the moment AI-generated code is quite far from that bar --- so anything AI-generated usually needs extensive clean-up.

To give some context (which you may or may not know already): this zulip has seen a lot of posts recently "I formalised X using AI, my code is at the corresponding level, I'm not interested in learning Lean myself, now please review my code". They get promptly deleted now (low-effort AI posts are disallowed; we want to keep this forum at a certain quality bar). It gets old after a while. Many people love to help genuinely interested learners, but not those who only feed that feedback directly to an AI without thinking. (It's more common than I'd like.)

Your case seems different - but it might be helpful to avoid the other impression :-)
(I'm not an algebraic geometer, so cannot comment on your specific question well. But I hope others will do so!)

Hi! I certainly understand this concern. In our case, most of the code was written either by hand or with Github Copilot on. In the latter case, we did benefit from line-level autocompletion, but not full scale auto-formalization. This was more useful in some places than others. But, at least for the parts I wrote myself, I have tinkered with the code at each line. The other use of generative AI that may be important to identify: most of the docstrings were written with the aid of Claude code (I asked it to propose a docstring for each function, and then I either accepted it or edited/rewrote it myself). And we did also use AI for some editing after the code type-checked. For example, I sometimes wrote a helper lemma after realizing I'd written the same couple lines over and over again, and then used AI to go back and wire in that lemma where it was useful.

Full disclosure, I did try using Aristotle and some other tools a couple times to see if it could clear hurdles, but always ended up rewriting the code myself because I either didn't like it or didn't think I could maintain it. I don't believe any code remains that was completely written by an AI agent.
Thanks for clarifying and for being honest about this! If there's a human actively trying to understand, that is reassuring.
I can share some abstract tips for making your code more mathlib-like: in January, I talked about that in an intro to Lean lecture in Bonn; the file I used is here. I hope this can be helpful!
